**Who this page is for.** Readers who know some dynamics and control but
not set-based verification. It condenses the explanatory chapter of the
project's technical report. Every pendulum number and figure on this page
comes from two short scripts that call the certifier's own set operations,
so the pendulum runs the same code as the lift. Each idea is shown on the
pendulum first; a shaded box then says what the same idea is **on the
lift**.

**The lift, in one paragraph.** A block rests on the floor in front of a
step. A disk, too weak to carry the block, must get it onto the step. It
does so indirectly: it pushes the block against the step's corner so that
the block tilts about its floor corner (the **pivot**), then pushes it up
and over so that it lands on the step in motion (the **landing**), and
finally slides it into place. The plan is a chain of pieces, and each piece
comes with a feedback law and a certificate.
[See [Certified funnels](../planar-build/funnels.qmd) for the chain.]{.details}

## 1. The question: what does it mean to certify a motion?

A test runs one starting state and watches what happens. A **certificate**
is a statement about *every* state in a set: for every starting state in
the piece's entry set, every disk friction in the declared band and every
disturbance in a measured set, the motion stays inside a tube, the contacts
behave as planned, and the motion leaves through an exit set that lies
inside the next piece's entry set. Pieces then chain by set containment.

**Why a simulator alone cannot do this.** A simulator runs one state at a
time, and a set holds infinitely many. Between two samples the motion can
change in kind: two landings a millimetre apart can end one with the block
sticking on the step corner and landing, the other with the block slipping
back to the floor.
[details: [issue #63](https://github.com/RobotControlLab/certified-contact-graphs/issues/63)]{.details}
No number of samples rules out a third, unsampled outcome. So the
certificates push *whole sets* of states through a model whose step can be
bounded, and the simulator is used for what it does well: measuring how far
the model is from it (Section 9).

## 2. The running example

A rigid pendulum of length $l = 1$ m swings under gravity with a torque $u$
(per unit inertia), $\theta = 0$ hanging down:
$$
\ddot\theta = -\tfrac{g}{l}\sin\theta + u, \qquad |u| \le u_{\max} = 4\ \text{rad/s}^2 .
$$
Its energy per unit inertia is $E = \tfrac12\dot\theta^2 - \tfrac{g}{l}\cos\theta$.
Without input the energy is constant and the state moves along a level
curve of $E$. One level is special: $E^* = g/l$ passes through the upright
$\theta = \pm\pi$ with zero speed. The orbit on it, the **homoclinic
orbit**, approaches the upright and takes infinitely long to get there. On
it the speed is a function of the angle,
$$
\dot\theta = \pm\,\omega(\theta), \qquad \omega(\theta) = 2\sqrt{g/l}\,\cos(\theta/2),
$$
6.26 rad/s at the bottom and zero at the top.

**The law.** Åström and Furuta's energy shaping [@astrom2000swinging] pumps
energy in until the state reaches that orbit:
$$
u = \operatorname{sat}\big(k\,(E^* - E)\,\dot\theta\big), \qquad k = 0.1,
$$
where $\operatorname{sat}$ clips to $\pm u_{\max}$. Physically: push along
the motion while the energy is too low, against it while it is too high.
Since $\dot E = \dot\theta\,u$, the unsaturated law gives
$\dot E = k\,(E^* - E)\,\dot\theta^2$, which moves $E$ toward $E^*$ and
stops only when the pendulum is at rest. From near the bottom the swing
grows for 5 to 10 s until the orbit is reached.

**The step.** The model is stepped the way the simulator (MuJoCo) steps:
semi-implicit Euler with $h = 10$ ms, velocity first, then position with the
new velocity:
$$
\dot\theta^+ = \dot\theta + h\big(-\tfrac{g}{l}\sin\theta + u\big), \qquad \theta^+ = \theta + h\,\dot\theta^+ .
$$
The certificate is a statement about this map, call it $F$, just as the
lift's certificates are statements about its 10 ms rigid step.

| Concept | Pendulum | The lift (the pivot) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| model that is propagated | rigid pendulum, semi-implicit Euler | reduced rigid contact model, same step |
| target motion | homoclinic orbit $\dot\theta = \omega(\theta)$ | a designed orbit $\dot\theta = \omega(\theta)$ |
| progress variable (where along the motion) | $\theta$, while $\dot\theta > 0$ | the block's tilt $\theta$ |
| transverse coordinate (distance from the target) | $E - E^*$, or $\eta = \dot\theta - \omega(\theta)$ | $\eta = \dot\theta - \omega(\theta)$, and the disk's place on the face |
| law | energy shaping | a push $c = c^* + K_\eta\,\eta + K_k\,(k - k^*)$ |
| modes | saturated or not | each contact sticking, sliding or open |
| what the model leaves out | bearing friction, a lagging motor | the simulator's soft contacts, penetration, solver |

: The pendulum and the lift, side by side. {#tbl-map}

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift: the reduced model.** The block and the disk have five
coordinates (the block's position and tilt, the disk's position). On one
piece of the plan, which contacts are closed is given by the plan, and so
is each contact's mode: a contact slides only where the geometry forces it
to, and in that direction; otherwise it sticks. Each closed contact pins
one combination of coordinates (its gap stays zero), and each sticking
contact pins another (its material point does not slide). On the pivot
these constraints leave the block a single free coordinate, its tilt. The
rigid-body equations along that one-coordinate family are three linear
equations in three unknowns (the tilt's acceleration and the two normal
forces), solved in closed form; a unique solution in this mode exists
exactly when their determinant is nonzero, and that is checked. Like
"a rigid pendulum with a torque", this is a deliberate reduction: rigid
bodies, one fixed mode per piece, a disk that does not roll. Everything
left out becomes a disturbance that is *measured* (Section 9).
:::

## 3. One step: pushing a set through the map

A certificate speaks about every state in a set, so the basic operation is:
given a set of states, compute a set that surely contains all their images
after one step.

**Zonotopes, in plain words.** A zonotope is a centre $c$ plus a few
arrows (the **generators**, the columns of a matrix $G$), each scaled by its
own weight between $-1$ and $1$:
$$
Z = \{\, c + G\xi \;:\; \xi \in [-1, 1]^m \,\}.
$$
With two arrows in the plane it is a parallelogram; with more, a centrally
symmetric polygon. A box is the special case with the arrows along the
axes. A linear map takes a zonotope to a zonotope exactly: the centre moves
and the arrows are stretched and turned.

**The straight-line guess.** Near the centre the step is almost linear:
$F(z) \approx F(c) + J_c\,(z - c)$, with $J_c$ the Jacobian at the centre.
Applied to the zonotope, this guess gives another zonotope,
$F(c) + J_c G\,\xi$. It is exact at the centre and gets worse away from it.

**What $R$ is.** $R$ is the **error margin of the straight-line guess**: a
number per coordinate that bounds how far the true image can be from the
guess, anywhere in the set. It is

> (how much the slope anywhere in the set can differ from the slope at the centre) $\times$ (how far the set reaches from the centre).

The enclosure is "the straight-line image, plus or minus $R$", and
$[-R, R]$ is appended as new generators, so that later steps turn it along
with the rest instead of boxing it.

**The formula.** The slope "anywhere in the set" is an **interval
Jacobian** $[J]$: a matrix of intervals, each containing that partial
derivative at every state of the set's bounding box. It is computed by
interval arithmetic on the step's own code, with outward rounding
[@harapanahalli2024immrax]. It is a slope bound for *this* set, never a
global Lipschitz constant. Then
$$
F(Z) \subseteq F(c) + J_c G\,\xi \;\oplus\; [-R, R], \qquad R = \big|[J] - J_c\big|\,\big(|G|\,\mathbf 1\big) + \text{rounding}.
$$
Why this is sound: by the mean value theorem, row by row,
$F_i(z) - F_i(c) = \nabla F_i(\zeta)\cdot(z - c)$ for *some* point $\zeta$
between $c$ and $z$. That point is **never computed**. It lies in the
bounding box, and $[J]$ covers the Jacobian at every point of the box, so
whatever $\zeta$ is, its slope differs from the centre's by at most a row of
$|[J] - J_c|$. Only computable pieces enter: $F(c)$ and $J_c$ (one
evaluation each), $[J]$ and $G$. The pessimism comes from using the box's
worst slope in place of the unknown $\zeta$. (A one-line warm-up: for
$f(x) = x^2$ on $[1, 3]$, $f(c) = 4$, $J_c = 4$, $[J] = [2, 6]$, so $R = 2$
and the enclosure is $[-2, 10]$, which contains the true image $[1, 9]$.)

**On the pendulum.** Take the box $\theta \in [0.25, 0.35]$ rad,
$\dot\theta \in [0.4, 0.6]$ rad/s near the bottom: $c = (0.3, 0.5)$,
$G = \operatorname{diag}(0.05, 0.1)$. Over this box the law's argument stays
in $[0.75, 1.15]$, well inside $\pm 4$, so the step is the smooth,
unsaturated map (Section 6 says how that is proved). The pieces:

- the centre's image $F(c) = (0.3048, 0.4805)$;
- the Jacobian at the centre and the interval Jacobian over the box,
  $$
  J_c = \begin{bmatrix} 0.99905 & 0.010188 \\ -0.09517 & 1.01881 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
  [J] = \begin{bmatrix} [0.99903,\ 0.99907] & [0.010185,\ 0.010191] \\ [-0.09707,\ -0.09312] & [1.01849,\ 1.01908] \end{bmatrix};
  $$
- the slope spread $|[J] - J_c|$ times the reach $|G|\mathbf 1 = (0.05, 0.1)$
  gives $R = (1.3\cdot 10^{-6},\ 1.3\cdot 10^{-4})$;
- the new generators $J_c G$: the box is sheared, because the angle picks up
  $h\dot\theta$ and the speed picks up gravity's pull, plus the two
  remainder generators $\operatorname{diag}(R)$.

The enclosure contains the true images of all 4,004 sampled states,
corners included. The largest actual error of the straight-line guess is
$0.31\,R$: $R$ is a bound, safe and pessimistic, not the error itself.

::: {.column-page-right}
![One 10 ms step from a box near the bottom. **(a)** The box (grey), the true images of sampled states (dots), the straight-line image $F(c) + J_cG\xi$ (dashed) and the enclosure with $\pm R$ appended (blue): the box has become a slightly sheared parallelogram. **(b)** A zoom at one corner: the true image of the box's edge (black) lies between the dashed parallelogram and the blue outer edge; that thin band is $R$. **(c)** The actual error of the straight-line guess in $\dot\theta^+$ over all samples, against $\pm R$ (red): every error is inside, with room to spare.](media/pz-one-step.svg){#fig-one-step}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift.** Within one contact mode, one 10 ms step of the reduced
model running its law is an explicit smooth formula, and each set is pushed
through it the same way. The step's code is evaluated in affine arithmetic
[@defigueiredo2004affine], with a rigorous remainder for each elementary
operation and outward rounding; an operation without such a rule raises an
error instead of passing silently. A piece starts from one entry set: a box
of states written as a zonotope (six coordinates on the landing).
:::

## 4. Many steps: rotation, growth and reduction

Repeat: each step maps the current zonotope and appends two remainder
generators. @fig-many-steps follows the box above for 134 steps (1.34 s),
while the pendulum swings from $\theta = 0.3$ to $-1$ rad and back. The set
stretches, because the pumping amplifies small differences in amplitude, and
it turns with the swing. At step 134 the set touches the curve where the
input saturates, its mode can no longer be proved, and the run stops there.

- **Generators pile up.** Without reduction the count is $2 + 2k$: 270
  generators at step 134.
- **Girard's reduction** [@girard2005reachability] keeps the generators that
  boxing would hurt most and replaces the rest by a small box. This is sound
  (the result still contains the set) and costs some tightness: with at most
  8 generators the area at step 134 is 1.07, against 0.53 unreduced and
  0.17 for the sampled states' convex hull (an inner estimate of the true
  set).
- **Boxes fail where zonotopes don't.** Replacing the set by its bounding
  box after every step (plain interval propagation) loses so much that at
  step 25 its area is 0.150 against the zonotope's 0.034, and at step 46 it
  can no longer prove the mode at all. A box cannot represent a tilted set,
  so each step re-wraps a tilted set in a larger upright box: the
  *wrapping effect*.

::: {.column-page-right}
![Many steps. **(a)** The zonotope (at most 8 generators) every 25 steps, the re-boxed sets (dashed, until they fail at step 46), sampled trajectories, and the saturation's switching curve. **(b)** Areas: the sampled hull, the zonotope without and with reduction, and the re-boxed set, which blows up first. **(c)** Generator counts: linear growth without reduction, a fixed cap with it.](media/pz-many-steps.svg){#fig-many-steps}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift.** The landing's impact window, a handful of 10 ms steps in
which the block hits the step, is where boxes fail and zonotopes succeed. It
is certified on all 16,384 units of its six-dimensional entry set: 310,372
certified pieces and none left uncertified. Re-boxing after every step would
need about $2^{36}$ pieces.
[See [Background: zonotope propagation](../planar-build/zonotopes.qmd).]{.details}
:::

## 5. Splitting: why smaller sets are much tighter

$R$ is (slope spread) $\times$ (reach), and *both* factors shrink in
proportion to the set's size. So $R$ grows with the **square** of the size:
halving the box quarters $R$ while only halving the straight-line part. On
the pendulum the fitted slope of $\log R$ against $\log(\text{size})$ is
2.01 over seven halvings, from $1.3\cdot 10^{-4}$ down to
$7.8\cdot 10^{-9}$ rad/s.

So cutting a box into pieces and propagating each piece separately gives a
tighter union. From a box 1.5 times the size of the one above, after 60
steps, the pieces' summed area over the sampled hull's area is 1.65 for one
piece, 1.25 for 4, 1.11 for 16 and 1.06 for 64. The price is the number of
pieces, which grows exponentially with the dimension. Splitting where needed,
and only there, is **branch and prune**.

::: {.column-page-right}
![Splitting. **(a)** The remainder $R$ (slope 2 on log-log axes) and the straight-line part (slope 1) against the box's size: small sets are almost linear. **(b)** After 60 steps: one box propagated whole (orange) against 16 sub-boxes each propagated on its own (blue), with sampled states. **(c)** Summed area of the pieces over the sampled hull's area, falling toward 1 as the pieces shrink.](media/pz-splitting.png){#fig-splitting}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift.** The landing certifies with pieces between $2^{-4}$ and
$2^{-8}$ of the entry box per coordinate, chosen by branch and prune.
Splitting every coordinate to the finest size everywhere would need about
$10^{10}$ pieces.
[See [Background: techniques that made the chain certify](../planar-build/certification-techniques.qmd).]{.details}
:::

## 6. Modes: exclusion, not bounding

The enclosure of Section 3 needs a smooth map. A step that switches mode
inside the set (the input saturates for some states and not others; a
contact sticks for some and slides for others) is not smooth there. The
certifier **never bounds across a switch; it excludes it.** Over the whole
set it proves that one mode's conditions hold, so nothing discontinuous
happens inside the certified set. Where that cannot be shown, it splits the
set or refuses it.

**On the pendulum, saturation is the mode switch.** Before each step the
law's argument $k(E^* - E)\dot\theta$ is bounded over the current set (the
same enclosure, applied to that one scalar):

- its whole range inside $(-u_{\max}, u_{\max})$: the step is the
  unsaturated map;
- its whole range above $u_{\max}$ (or below $-u_{\max}$): the step is the
  saturated map $u = \pm u_{\max}$, also smooth;
- otherwise the set straddles the switching curve: refused, and the entry
  box is split and each piece tried again, down to a largest depth.

@fig-modes takes an entry box 30 steps before the swing reaches saturation
and an 80-step horizon in which the pendulum enters and leaves the saturated
region. No piece certifies at depths 0 to 3: every one straddles at some
step. At depth 10, 167 pieces certify, each with a single mode at every step
(saturation starting at step 29, 30 or 31), and 140 are refused. The
certified fraction of the entry box grows with depth: 0.13 at depth 4, 0.53
at 6, 0.73 at 8, 0.86 at 10. The refused pieces form thin bands, the entry
states whose motion lands right on the switching curve at some step. They
shrink with depth but never vanish, because those states really do switch
"inside" any set around them.

::: {.column-page-right}
![Saturation as a mode. **(a)** The entry box after branch and prune: certified pieces (blue; the shade gives the step at which saturation starts, 29 to 31) and refused pieces (red), in thin bands. **(b)** Every piece's set at step 60, where the swing leaves saturation: each certified piece is wholly unsaturated (blue) or wholly saturated (orange); pieces refused at this step straddle the switching curve (red); gaps are pieces refused earlier. **(c)** The uncertified fraction of the entry box against the tree's largest depth.](media/pz-modes.svg){#fig-modes}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift, the modes are the contacts', and the conditions are
physical.** Over each set the certificate proves: every closed contact
presses with at least a minimum normal force; every sticking contact's force
lies strictly inside its friction cone (the disk's at the low end, 0.3, of
its friction band); every sliding contact slips in its planned direction and
no faster than a measured bound; and the mode's determinant is nonzero. The
other modes are excluded too: on the pivot, all 15 alternatives (each
environment contact sliding or opening, the disk sticking, sliding either
way or opening) are excluded on every one of its 3,521 bands. At the
landing every unplanned contact class is excluded at every step of the
impact window.
[See [Background: the contact-class solve](../planar-build/contact-class-solve.qmd).]{.details}
:::

## 7. The tube around an orbit

**The progress variable.** On the homoclinic orbit with $\dot\theta > 0$
the angle keeps increasing, so $\theta$ itself can say "where along the
swing" we are, without a clock. The target becomes a function of $\theta$,
$\dot\theta = \omega(\theta)$, and the distance from it is the **transverse
coordinate** $\eta = \dot\theta - \omega(\theta)$. On the energy level the
two measures are tied: $E - E^* = \omega\eta + \eta^2/2$. (During the
pumping, $\theta$ swings back and forth and indexes nothing; so the tube
below covers one swing near the orbit, from $\theta_0 = -2.6$ to
$\theta_1 = 2.6$ rad, where $\dot\theta$ stays above 1.3 rad/s.)

**The law contracts the transverse coordinate per unit of progress.**
Dividing $\dot E$ by $\dot\theta$,
$$
\frac{d(E - E^*)}{d\theta} = -k\,\dot\theta\,(E - E^*),
$$
so over one swing the energy error shrinks by a factor of about 0.09.

**The tube, indexed by progress.** Cut $[\theta_0, \theta_1]$ into 473
narrow bands. Each band holds an interval of $\eta$. The image of each band
under one step is enclosed as in Section 3 and added to the bands it
reaches, all of them later bands, because $\theta$ advances by more than a
band's width per step (so one forward pass computes the tube). On every
band two things are checked: the unsaturated mode (smallest margin 3.67 of
the 4 rad/s² available) and the advance (smallest margin 0.0033 rad). From
$\eta \in [-0.3, 0.3]$ rad/s (an energy error of $\pm 0.61$), the tube
narrows to $[-0.026, 0.061]$ at the bottom and leaves through
$[-0.156, 0.041]$. All 200 sampled trajectories stay inside it.

**Indexed by time, the same set spreads along the orbit.** Propagated as
sets at fixed times, the states that started slightly faster run ahead; the
set stretches along the orbit (its $\theta$ spread reaches 1.17 rad), and
because the orbit is curved, the convex set's $\eta$ range blows up to
about $\pm 4$ rad/s near the top, where the mode can no longer be proved.
Nothing pulls the states together *along* the path, so a certificate that
does not depend on a clock should not carry that direction as a coordinate.
That is why the lift's tubes are indexed by a progress variable.

::: {.column-page-right}
![The transverse view of one swing. **(a)** The tube indexed by progress, in $(\theta, \eta)$ (aqua), stays narrow; the bounding boxes of the time-indexed sets from the same entry set (violet, every 6 steps) grow; sampled trajectories (lines) stay in the tube. **(b)** The tube's bound on the energy error $E - E^*$ and the trajectories' energy errors: the spread shrinks along the swing (the common wiggle is the time step's own energy error). **(c)** Half-widths: the tube's $\eta$, against the time-indexed set's $\eta$ and $\theta$.](media/pz-transverse.svg){#fig-transverse}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift.** On the pivot the progress variable is the block's tilt,
and the certificate checks that the tilt keeps increasing at a positive
minimum rate over the whole tube. The target orbit is not given by physics:
it is *designed*, as a tilt rate $\omega(\theta)$ chosen so that each
sliding contact slips no faster than a rate measured in the simulator, with
the contact nearest its limit dominating (like resistors in parallel). The
law reads the tilt, not a clock:
$c = c^*(\theta) + K_\eta(\theta)\,\eta + K_k(\theta)\,(k - k^*)$, a push
along a fixed direction. Here $c^*$ is the push that follows the orbit
exactly, and the gains are chosen from a linearization so that, to first
order, $\dot\eta = -\lambda\eta$. The linearization is for design only: the
tube is computed on the full nonlinear model running this exact law, so a
linearization error can make the tube loose but never the certificate
false. The pivot's tube has 3,521 bands and a transverse half-width of
0.91°/s in tilt rate. This is maneuver regulation with transverse
coordinates [@hauser1995maneuver; @shiriaev2010transverse;
@manchester2011transverse], and the tubes compose by "exit set inside the
next entry set" [@burridge1999sequential].
[See [Background: certified funnels and composition](../planar-build/funnel-composition.qmd).]{.details}
:::

## 8. Sampling versus sets

Sample 1000 starting states uniformly in the box
$\theta \in [-0.1, 0.1]$, $\dot\theta \in [-0.2, 0.2]$ and run the closed
loop for 12 s. All 1000 reach the orbit ($|E - E^*| \le 0.25$), in 5.3 to
9.9 s. From 1000 successes out of 1000, the Clopper–Pearson bound
[@clopper1934use] says: with 95% confidence, at most 0.3% of the box fails.
That statement is true.

But the box contains the equilibrium $(0, 0)$, where $u = 0$ and the
pendulum never moves, and states near it take arbitrarily long to get going.
A fine grid gives the true failing fraction for a time budget $T$: 0.056 at
8 s, $1.2\cdot 10^{-3}$ at 10 s, $2.4\cdot 10^{-5}$ at 12 s. It is never
zero, and 1000 samples never see it. The statement "every state of this box
reaches the orbit within 12 s" is false, so no certificate of it can exist,
and the set computation agrees: no enclosure of a set containing the
equilibrium can prove progress there.

::: {.column-page-right}
![Sampling. **(a)** 1000 starts, coloured by the time to reach the orbit. The states that fail within 12 s are around the equilibrium and too small to see; those that fail within 8 s lie inside the orange spiral. **(b)** Twelve rollouts, with their saturated stretches in orange. **(c)** The true failing fraction of the box against the time budget (from a fine grid), and the 95% bound that 1000 successes give: right as a probability, silent about the states that fail.](media/pz-montecarlo.png){#fig-montecarlo}
:::

Rollouts give a **probabilistic** certificate: a statement about random
starts drawn from a stated distribution [@calafiore2006scenario;
@devonport2020scenario]. That is the right tool when the question is a
probability, and the wrong tool when the question is "every state of this
set", which is what chaining pieces needs.

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift.** The simulator's step (MJX, the JAX version of MuJoCo) has
an iterative soft-contact solver and branches on contact detection, so
there is no usable enclosure of a set through it. The design therefore
proves set statements on a model it can bound and uses statistics only for
the model–simulator gap. What this buys:

- **Every state, not random ones.** A junction certifies that a whole exit
  set lies inside the next entry set. A statement about random starts does
  not chain: the next piece's starts are wherever this piece's motions end,
  not distributed like its samples.
- **Composition does not degrade.** Sixteen junctions at a failure
  probability $\epsilon$ each could cost $16\epsilon$; set containment
  composes exactly.
- **The statistics are small, rich and reusable.** One quantity, the
  one-step residual (next section), which every simulated step samples and
  which carries over to other entry sets, laws and pieces with the same
  contacts.
- **It explains itself.** Each condition comes with its margin, so a
  failure says which constraint binds.

The costs: conservative bounds, expensive splitting, the need for a rigid
model close to the simulator, and a statistical residual. Simulation-based
funnels exist too [@reist2016simlqr]; theirs are probabilistic, these are
proved on the model.
:::

## 9. The bridge to the simulator: the residual $\mathcal W$

Neither the pendulum's model nor the lift's rigid model is the system that
actually runs. The certificate covers the running system without
propagating it, in four steps:

1. **Write the true step in terms of the model's step:**
   $x^+_{\text{true}} = F(x) + w$. The **one-step residual** $w$ collects
   everything the model leaves out. In the simulator: penetration,
   compliance, solver tolerance.
2. **Measure $w$; do not propagate it.** Along many rollouts of the true
   system, compare each true step with the model's step from the same state:
   one model evaluation per step, no sets. A 95/95 bound (covering 95% of
   rollouts with 95% confidence) gives the disturbance set $\mathcal W$.
3. **Propagate the model with $\mathcal W$ over sets:**
   $X_{k+1} \supseteq F(X_k) \oplus \mathcal W$, an enclosure plus a
   Minkowski sum per step. This is the certified tube: it contains every
   motion of "model plus any disturbance in $\mathcal W$ at every step".
4. **Coverage.** A true motion *is* a model motion driven by its own
   residuals. If each residual lies in $\mathcal W$, the true motion stays
   in the tube.

So the guarantee has **two layers**:

- *Proved:* if the residuals lie in $\mathcal W$, the true system stays in
  the tube.
- *Measured:* the residuals lie in $\mathcal W$, at 95/95; and held-out
  rollouts are checked to stay inside.

**On the pendulum.** The "true" pendulum adds what the model leaves out:
bearing friction ($b = 0.01$ 1/s) and a motor that delivers the commanded
torque through a 30 ms lag. Each of 600 calibration rollouts starts near the
orbit, and every step gives a residual (76,944 steps). For each rollout take
the largest $|w|$ per coordinate; over the 600 rollouts, the 580th smallest
bounds 95% of rollouts at 95% confidence (Wilks' order statistic
[@wilks1941tolerance]). That gives
$\mathcal W = [\pm 6.1\cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{rad}] \times [\pm 6.1\cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{rad/s}]$.

- The tube of Section 7 with $\mathcal W$ added at every step still
  certifies.
- Of 600 new rollouts, **all 600 stay in the tube computed with
  $\mathcal W$**, against 225 in the tube of the ideal model alone: the
  friction's steady drag pulls the rest out.
- In 584 of the 600, every residual lies in $\mathcal W$; in the other 16,
  some residual is just outside. Those 16 still stay in the tube, because
  the tube is a worst case over $\mathcal W$ at every step, which a real
  sequence of residuals never attains.

::: {.column-page-right}
![The residual. **(a)** One-step residuals on the edge, with $\mathcal W$ (from per-rollout maxima, 95/95) and the smaller per-step 95/95 box. **(b)** The tube of the ideal model (aqua) and of the ideal model plus $\mathcal W$ (blue), with held-out rollouts of the true pendulum: the second tube holds them all, the first does not. **(c)** The per-rollout maxima of the speed residual and the order statistic that sets the bound.](media/pz-residual.png){#fig-residual}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift.** On the pivot the residual is an extra term on the tilt
acceleration, bounded at 0.556 rad/s² from 4,000 simulator rollouts, plus a
measured creep bound of 0.116 mm. Of the held-out
rollouts that entered the entry set, 971 of 971 (disk friction 0.5) and 967
of 968 (friction 0.3) stayed in the tube; the tube without the measured
residual and creep contained none of them entirely. On the wide transport
piece, 731 of 731 held-out rollouts that entered the funnel stayed inside;
49 of 780 did not enter, because a quantity the plan holds fixed while a
contact sticks (a constant of motion) creeps on the way in, and all 49 still completed the transport.
[details: [issue #77](https://github.com/RobotControlLab/certified-contact-graphs/issues/77)]{.details}
The guarantee is therefore conditional and about the simulator; about
hardware it says nothing until the same residuals are measured there.
:::

**The weak points, stated.**

- **The 5% tail.** The bound covers 95% of rollouts at 95% confidence, not
  all. A rollout in the tail is not covered, though it usually stays inside
  (the pendulum's 16). Scenario or conformal bounds could state the level
  more sharply.
- **Independence.** The statistic is a maximum per whole rollout, so it
  needs only independent rollouts. But the states a tube visits are not
  distributed like the calibration starts, so the sampled residuals are not
  clearly representative of every state in the tube.
- **The model's blind spots.** Compliance enters only as a disturbance;
  the disk does not roll; one fixed mode per piece (a stick planned at the
  step corner can slip in the simulator).
  [details: [issue #63](https://github.com/RobotControlLab/certified-contact-graphs/issues/63)]{.details}

**How it could improve.** Move compliance into the model (penetration as
geometry), which shrinks $\mathcal W$; make $\mathcal W$ state-dependent;
or, a research direction, reduce the simulator's own contact model: for a
fixed set of active contacts its step is one linear solve, an explicit
smooth map like the reduced model's, which could be propagated and
certified per active set, shrinking $\mathcal W$ to solver tolerance. The
closest formal analogue of $\mathcal W$ is a simulation-gap function treated
as a disturbance [@sangeerth2024simgap]; checking "model plus $\mathcal W$"
on held-out runs is reachset conformance [@roehm2016reachset;
@tang2023contact].

## 10. Control barrier functions on the pendulum

The tubes above certify that the motion *follows a plan*. A **barrier**
certifies something different: that the motion *never enters a set of bad
states*, whatever else it does. Two things must be kept apart throughout:

- an **online safety filter**, which at every step solves a small
  optimization to pick an input that respects the barrier condition *at
  the current state*; and
- a **verified barrier certificate**, which proves over a whole set that
  such an input exists at every state of it.

### The requirement and its barriers

**The requirement:** keep the swing below an amplitude,
$|\theta| \le \theta_{\max} = 1$ rad. A **barrier function** $h$ turns it
into a set: the safe set is $\{x : h(x) \ge 0\}$
[@ames2017cbf; @ames2019cbf]. Four barriers express the requirement (or a
stronger one) differently:

- **Energy**, $h_E = E_{\max} - E$ with $E_{\max} = -\tfrac{g}{l}\cos\theta_{\max}$:
  the region inside the unpowered pendulum's swing of amplitude
  $\theta_{\max}$. The input appears directly in its rate,
  $\dot h_E = -\dot\theta\,u$ ("relative degree one").
- **Angle, quadratic**, $h_Q = \theta_{\max}^2 - \theta^2$: its rate
  $-2\theta\dot\theta$ does not contain $u$, so a *high-order* barrier is
  needed [@xiao2022hocbf]: the condition is imposed on
  $\psi_1 = \dot h + \alpha_1 h$, whose rate does contain $u$.
- **Angle, linear**, $h_L = \theta_{\max} \mp \theta$, one per side, each
  with its high-order barrier ($\alpha_1 = 2$, $\alpha_2 = 10$).
- **Braking**, $h_B$: built from the motion full braking produces. Under
  $u = -u_{\max}$ the quantity
  $E_u = \tfrac12\dot\theta^2 - \tfrac{g}{l}\cos\theta + u_{\max}\theta$ is
  constant, so $h_B \ge 0$ exactly when full braking stops the swing before
  $\theta_{\max}$ (and its mirror image for the other direction). Full
  braking always satisfies its condition.

::: {.column-page-right}
![Safe sets in the phase plane, for $\theta_{\max} = 1$ rad and $u_{\max} = 4$. **(a)** The viability kernel (aqua: the states from which full braking stops the swing in time), the energy barrier's boundary (blue), the linear high-order set (orange) and the braking barrier's boundary (green, dashed), which sits on the kernel's edge. **(b)** The quadratic high-order set: unbounded in speed at $\theta = 0$, where $h_Q$'s gradient vanishes.](media/cbf-safe-sets.svg){#fig-cbf-sets}
:::

### The condition and the safety filter

**The condition** is $\dot h(x, u) \ge -\alpha\,h(x)$: the barrier may
decrease, but never faster than in proportion to its own value, so it can
approach zero and never cross it ($h(t) \ge h(0)\,e^{-\alpha t}$). On the
pendulum each condition is affine in the one input, $a(x)\,u \ge b(x)$.

**The filter** takes the nominal input (the energy pumping) and changes it
as little as possible:
$$
\min_u\ (u - u_{\text{nom}})^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad a_i(x)\,u \ge b_i(x)\ \text{for every barrier}, \quad |u| \le u_{\max}.
$$
With one input the allowed inputs form an interval, and the answer is
$u_{\text{nom}}$ clipped to it. If the interval is empty, the filter is
*infeasible*. It runs every 10 ms on the sampled state. From $(0.1, 0)$ for
12 s:

- **unfiltered**, the pumping reaches the homoclinic orbit and the swing
  goes over the top;
- **filtered by $h_L$**, the swing is held to 0.61 rad: with these $\alpha$'s
  the condition is conservative and stops the pumping well short of the
  limit;
- **filtered by $h_B$**, the swing reaches 0.975 rad, braking hard at each
  end;
- **filtered by $h_E$**, the energy settles at $E_{\max}$ and the swing at
  0.998 rad. Its smallest $h_E$ is $-0.066$: the continuous-time condition,
  applied every 10 ms, lets the sampled system overshoot slightly. That is
  why the project states its barriers in discrete time,
  $h(x_{k+1}) - h(x_k) \ge -\gamma\,h(x_k)$ [@agrawal2017discrete].

No step of these runs was infeasible.

::: {.column-page-right}
![The safety filter on top of the energy pumping, from $(0.1, 0)$. **(a)** The angle limit: unfiltered (grey, out to the homoclinic orbit), filtered by $h_L$ (orange, stops well inside the limit) and by $h_B$ (green, reaches the limit), with their safe sets' boundaries. **(b)** The energy limit: filtered by $h_E$ (blue), settling on the swing of amplitude 1 rad.](media/cbf-phase.svg){#fig-cbf-phase}
:::

::: {.column-page-right}
![Barrier values (top) and inputs (bottom) over time for the three filters. Yellow shading marks where the filter changes the nominal input (red would mark an infeasible step; none occurs). The barrier values approach zero and level off instead of crossing it.](media/cbf-time.svg){#fig-cbf-time}
:::

### Input limits and feasibility

The filter assumes that an admissible input meeting the condition exists.
With $|u| \le u_{\max}$ it may not: there can be "safe" states from which
every admissible input leads out. The **viability kernel** is the largest
set from which staying safe is possible; a barrier whose safe set reaches
outside it promises what no input can deliver.

- **$h_Q$ is degenerate.** Its gradient vanishes at $\theta = 0$, so the
  input's coefficient vanishes there too, and fast states at the bottom have
  no admissible input: 8.9 of the safe set's 23.7 (rad·rad/s) are
  infeasible. A barrier's gradient must not vanish where the condition is
  needed.
- **$h_L$ asks for more braking than the motor has** at the corners of its
  set: a state near one limit moving fast toward it is "safe" by the
  condition, but cannot be stopped in time. 1.09 of its 8.0 is infeasible.
  Tuning $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$ shrinks this (to 0.010 at $\alpha_2 = 160$) but
  never to zero, because gravity at the limit ($g\sin 1 = 8.25$) exceeds
  $u_{\max} = 4$.
- **$h_B$ is feasible everywhere** in its set, by construction: its safe
  set is the viability kernel (up to the time step), and full braking is
  always admissible. Building a barrier from the motion of a fixed backup
  input is the backup-controller construction [@gurriet2020scalable].

The lesson: choose the safe set so that the condition stays feasible under
the input limits; the most reliable way is to build it from a motion a fixed
admissible input produces, or from a quantity the unpowered system
conserves.

::: {.column-page-right}
![The admissible-input region. Colour: the width of the interval of inputs $|u| \le u_{\max}$ that meet the barrier condition, over the safe set (red: none). Yellow: the edge of the region where the nominal pumping input is not allowed, so the filter acts. Arrows: the unpowered motion. **(a)** $h_L$: red corners where the swing toward a limit is too fast to brake. **(b)** $h_B$: no red anywhere.](media/cbf-field.png){#fig-cbf-field}
:::

::: {.column-page-right}
![Feasibility under $|u| \le 4$. **(a)** $h_Q$: no input authority at $\theta = 0$, so a band of fast states at the bottom is infeasible. **(b)** $h_L$: infeasible corners; dashed, the viability kernel. **(c)** $h_L$'s infeasible fraction of its safe set against $\alpha_2$, for three values of $\alpha_1$: it falls but never reaches zero ($h_B$ has none).](media/cbf-feasibility.svg){#fig-cbf-feas}
:::

### Verifying a barrier over sets

The filter checks the condition at the current state only. A
**certificate** proves, over a whole set, that at every state some
admissible input meets it. The script does this with the certifier's own
enclosures and branch and prune over the box $[-1.05, 1.05] \times [-8, 8]$.
Each piece of the box ends up in one of four classes:

- **outside**: some barrier is proved negative on all of it, so there is
  nothing to show;
- **certified**: an admissible input is proved to meet the condition at
  every state of the piece's part of the safe set (for $h_B$, full braking
  on one side of $\dot\theta = 0$ makes that side's condition hold
  identically, and the other side's is proved by its enclosure);
- **proved infeasible**: the piece lies in the safe set and no admissible
  input can meet the condition anywhere in it;
- otherwise it is split, and at depth 10 **refused**.

For $h_L$: certified 7.6, refused 2.4 and proved infeasible 0.20
(rad·rad/s), the refused and infeasible pieces along the infeasible corners
and the set's edge. For $h_B$: certified 31.4 and refused 0.03, two tiny
pieces at the corners $(\pm 1, 0)$ where the condition is tight.

::: {.column-page-right}
![The barrier condition verified over boxes by branch and prune with the certifier's enclosures: certified (green), proved infeasible (red), refused at the largest depth (pink), proved outside the safe set (grey). **(a)** $h_L$: its infeasible corners show up as red and pink. **(b)** $h_B$: certified almost everywhere.](media/cbf-verified.svg){#fig-cbf-verified}
:::

Two caveats. The condition verified here is the continuous-time one; the
discrete-time form is checked the same way with the step map in place of
the derivative. And a certificate needs a model: the residual $\mathcal W$
enters as a disturbance, and what is then certified is input-to-state
safety [@kolathaya2019issf], the invariance of a safe set enlarged by the
residual's effect.

### Energy shaping with a barrier on top

With $h_E$, the filter turns "pump up to the homoclinic orbit" into "pump up
to $E_{\max}$, never beyond". For amplitudes of 1, 2 and 2.8 rad the energy
settles within 0.26 of $E_{\max}$. Every safe set $\{E \le E_{\max}\}$ with
$E_{\max} < E^*$ is bounded by a swing of the *unpowered* pendulum, so it is
invariant with $u = 0$, and the condition is feasible everywhere in it,
whatever $u_{\max}$ is. As $E_{\max} \to E^*$ the boundary approaches the
homoclinic orbit; beyond $E^*$ the set contains rotations over the top, and
an energy barrier can no longer limit the angle. This is the dissipativity
view: a storage function whose sublevel sets the uncontrolled system keeps
is a barrier for free.
[See [Background: dissipation certificates](../planar-build/passivity-certificates.qmd).]{.details}

::: {.column-page-right}
![Energy pumping filtered by $h_E$. **(a)** The energy over time for three safe energies (dotted lines) and unfiltered (rising to $E^*$, dashed): each filtered run levels off at its limit. **(b)** The last 3 s: the swings reached, nested inside the homoclinic orbit.](media/cbf-energy.svg){#fig-cbf-energy}
:::

::: {.on-lift}
**On the lift: the landing's barriers.** The landing (the block carried up
over the step corner and set down on the step) is checked as barrier
conditions in two phases.

- **The controlled phase: feasibility along the path.** While the disk can
  still push, a disk force within its limits must exist, at every pose along
  the landing, that keeps every barrier $h_i \ge 0$ with
  $\dot h_i \ge -\alpha(h_i)$. This is the pendulum's feasibility question,
  with the disk's force limits in place of $|u| \le u_{\max}$; the
  quasi-static condition "a balancing force exists" is its special case at
  zero speed. Each $h$ and $\alpha$ comes from a physical limit or a
  measurement, not a tuned value. The hard barriers are:
  - the block's spin rate stays bounded;
  - the disk's penetration into the block stays within its measured band;
  - the block stays on the step;
  - the disk stays away from the block's corners: the distance of the disk's
    contact point from the ends of the face, minus a margin derived from the
    measured placement and tracking errors.
    [details: [issue #73](https://github.com/RobotControlLab/certified-contact-graphs/issues/73)]{.details}

  The step corner's friction cone is *not* a barrier but a permitted mode
  switch: the block may stick or slip there. A slip must then end at rest in
  a formation from which the lift can continue (still on the corner, or slid
  back onto the floor): a reach-avoid condition with that fallback as the
  slip's target set. A landing is admitted unless an unsafe outcome is
  reachable. These conditions are currently checked by the existence of a
  force along the path; verified barrier certificates over sets, as in
  @fig-cbf-verified, are planned.
  [details: [issue #54](https://github.com/RobotControlLab/certified-contact-graphs/issues/54)]{.details}
- **The dynamic phase: an energy barrier.** From the first pose where no
  admissible force exists, the barrier is on a storage function,
  $h = E_{\text{rest}} - V(x)$: the block's energy above its landed rest, at
  touch-down, must be no larger than the level from which it is certified
  to come to rest on the step. This is the pendulum's $h_E$: a level of a
  storage function that the dissipative, unpowered motion keeps.

A simple screen of this second kind already runs on executed landings: it
rejects a landing whose peak kinetic energy exceeds
$m g(\varepsilon_{\text{pen}} + \varepsilon_{\text{on}})$, a small energy
budget: what the block would gain falling through the contact recognizer's tolerance band (its penetration limit plus its contact tolerance, 6 mm here). On 1,473 recorded
landing states it rejected all 19 unsafe landings and no other, where
barriers evaluated on the planned motion did not separate them.
[details: [issue #63](https://github.com/RobotControlLab/certified-contact-graphs/issues/63)]{.details}
:::

The distinction of this section carries over: a safety filter in the
controller is an online mechanism whose guarantees are only as good as the
condition's feasibility; a barrier certificate is a proof over sets on the
model, carried to the simulator through $\mathcal W$ like every other
certificate here. Safety filters in general are surveyed in
[@hsu2024safetyfilter]; a barrier filter with a learned residual in its
derivative, the barrier counterpart of $\mathcal W$, is
[@taylor2020learning].

## 11. The division of labour

| Job | Tool | Kind of statement |
|:--|:--|:--|
| enclose every state's motion in a piece | zonotope propagation of the rigid reduced model | proof, given $\mathcal W$ |
| exclude mode switches | mode conditions over sets, branch and prune | proof |
| chain pieces | exit set inside the next entry set | proof |
| bound the model–simulator gap | one-step residuals along simulator rollouts | 95/95 statistics |
| validate the combination | held-out simulator rollouts | counts, with confidence bounds |
| screen candidates fast | batched simulator rollouts | estimate, no certificate |

: Who does what. {#tbl-division}

**The statistics go to the smallest, most reusable place, the simulator's
one-step residual, and everything else is proved.** Simulator rollouts
remain the right tool for a fast screen, not for certificates.

## Further reading

- **Zonotopes and their reduction:** Girard [@girard2005reachability]; set
  arithmetic in JAX with immrax [@harapanahalli2024immrax]; affine
  arithmetic [@defigueiredo2004affine].
- **Tubes around orbits and their composition:** maneuver regulation
  [@hauser1995maneuver], transverse coordinates
  [@shiriaev2010transverse; @manchester2011transverse], sequential
  composition of funnels [@burridge1999sequential].
- **The swing-up law:** Åström and Furuta [@astrom2000swinging].
- **Statistics:** Wilks' tolerance limits [@wilks1941tolerance]; the
  scenario approach [@calafiore2006scenario].
- **Control barrier functions:** Ames et al. [@ames2019cbf], high-order
  barriers [@xiao2022hocbf], backup sets [@gurriet2020scalable], discrete
  time [@agrawal2017discrete], safety filters [@hsu2024safetyfilter].
- **Related ways to bridge a model and a simulator:** simulation-gap
  functions [@sangeerth2024simgap], reachset conformance
  [@roehm2016reachset], smoothing-error tubes for contact
  [@li2026tubes].
